inputs.need:
I am the anaesthetist who leads our prehabilitation program before major abdominal surgery (colorectal, upper gastrointestinal, liver and pancreatic resections). About 110 patients a quarter have these operations, but the supervised exercise program has 40 places a quarter. At the moment we decide who gets a place using cardiopulmonary exercise testing: patients with an anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min are prioritised. But we have one CPET machine, a four-week wait, and many patients have surgery within five weeks of the decision to operate, so half are never tested in time.

I want to know whether a simple bedside test done at the pre-assessment clinic could pick out the patients with a low anaerobic threshold well enough to allocate prehabilitation places. The candidates are the 30-second sit-to-stand test and gait speed over four metres, which our physiotherapists already use. My plan is a diagnostic accuracy study: consecutive patients booked for major abdominal surgery would do the bedside tests at pre-assessment and then CPET as the reference standard within two weeks, before any prehabilitation starts. I would like to know the sensitivity and specificity at useful cut-offs, and whether a combination is better than either test alone.

I need help with the sample size, choosing cut-offs without overfitting, dealing with patients who cannot complete CPET, making sure the testers are blind to each other's results, and deciding what accuracy would be good enough to replace CPET for triage. The physiotherapy department has agreed to run the tests; ethics approval has been applied for but not yet granted.
inputs.constraints: One CPET machine with 12 test slots a week. The bedside tests must take less than ten minutes at pre-assessment. No funding beyond existing staff time; results are needed within 12 months.

records.title: Accuracy of the 30-second sit-to-stand test for a low anaerobic threshold before major abdominal surgery
records.authors: Okonkwo-Brandvold T, Laurent-Mensah P, Ishikawa-Reid A
records.abstract: In 212 consecutive patients awaiting major abdominal surgery, the 30-second sit-to-stand test was compared with cardiopulmonary exercise testing. A count of 10 or fewer identified an anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min with sensitivity 78 percent and specificity 69 percent. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.77. Testers knew the exercise test results in a third of patients, and 14 patients who could not complete exercise testing were excluded. The cut-off was chosen in the same data, which may overstate accuracy in new patients.

records.title: Gait speed and anaerobic threshold in older surgical patients: a small comparison
records.abstract: In 64 patients aged 65 or older scheduled for major surgery, gait speed over four metres was compared with the anaerobic threshold from exercise testing. Gait speed below 1.0 m/s identified an anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min with sensitivity 71 percent and specificity 62 percent. The abstract does not state the year of the meeting, the recruitment period, how patients were selected or whether testers were blinded. The abstract gives no information about losses to follow-up or missing exercise tests.

records.title: Field tests of functional capacity against cardiopulmonary exercise testing before major surgery: a systematic review of diagnostic accuracy
records.authors: Rasmussen-Obi H, Petrakis-Nwosu D, Svensson-Achebe K, Tanaka-Holt R
records.abstract: We included 15 studies comparing simple field tests (sit-to-stand, gait speed, stair climbing, incremental shuttle walk) with the anaerobic threshold from exercise testing before major surgery. Sensitivity for a low anaerobic threshold ranged from 62 to 81 percent and specificity from 55 to 78 percent. Most studies were at high risk of bias in patient selection and blinding, and no study validated a cut-off in a separate sample. Patients unable to complete exercise testing were usually excluded. No field test was accurate enough to replace exercise testing for individual risk assessment.

records.title: Combining sit-to-stand and gait speed to triage patients for prehabilitation: a service report
records.authors: Surgical prehabilitation service, Kestrelmoor General Hospital
records.abstract: A single hospital combined the 30-second sit-to-stand test and gait speed to decide which patients were offered supervised prehabilitation. The service reports that most patients it judged high risk were identified by the combination, but exercise testing was done only in patients with abnormal bedside results, so accuracy cannot be calculated. Uptake of prehabilitation rose after the triage change. The report gives no date, no numbers for the patients tested and no description of how the combination rule was chosen.

records.title: Prehabilitation places, waiting times and postoperative complications at a regional surgical centre
records.abstract: Among 540 patients undergoing major abdominal surgery at one centre, those who completed at least four weeks of supervised prehabilitation had fewer postoperative complications than those who did not, but patients who completed the program were younger and fitter. Of patients prioritised for a place by exercise testing, 46 percent started prehabilitation too late to complete four weeks before surgery because they waited for the test. The authors argue that faster triage matters as much as the choice of triage test.

records.title: Patients unable to complete cardiopulmonary exercise testing before major surgery: frequency and outcomes
records.abstract: Of 1,120 patients referred for exercise testing before major surgery, 9 percent could not complete a test, most often because of joint pain, frailty or breathlessness at low workloads. These patients had the highest rate of postoperative complications in the cohort. Accuracy studies that excluded them would overstate the specificity of any bedside test, because the patients most likely to fail both tests are removed. The authors recommend a pre-specified rule that classifies inability to complete testing as low functional capacity.

records.title: Sample size for diagnostic accuracy studies when the target condition prevalence is uncertain: a practical guide
records.authors: Halvorsen-Adeyemi E, Quist-Morales R, Sato-Kowalczyk N
records.abstract: We give worked examples for planning accuracy studies. Estimating a sensitivity of 80 percent with a 95 percent confidence interval of plus or minus 10 percentage points needs about 62 patients with the target condition; if the prevalence is 40 percent, about 155 patients must be recruited. We recommend inflating the total for patients without a usable reference result, pre-specifying cut-offs from earlier studies, and reporting accuracy for a second cut-off only as exploratory. Choosing a cut-off in the same data inflates both sensitivity and specificity.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; two undated grey records are left unrated. One study found a sit-to-stand cut-off of 10 or fewer detected a low anaerobic threshold with sensitivity 78 and specificity 69 percent, but chose the cut-off in its own data. A review found field-test sensitivity of 62 to 81 percent, no validated cut-off and routine exclusion of patients who cannot complete exercise testing, which overstates specificity. Waiting for exercise testing delayed prehabilitation for almost half of prioritised patients elsewhere. The evidence supports a validation study of pre-specified cut-offs in consecutive patients, not a switch to bedside triage now.
response.gradeRationale: Single-centre accuracy studies with cut-offs derived in the same data, a review of studies at high risk of bias, and unappraisable grey reports; serious risk of bias and imprecision.
response.summary: Seven records appraised; two undated records left unrated with null scores; six claims.

response.reading: Triage is a race between the date of surgery and the time needed for testing and four weeks of prehabilitation. Exercise testing is the accepted reference but too slow; bedside tests are fast but their accuracy is uncertain and their published cut-offs were derived in their own data. The patients who cannot complete exercise testing are the frailest and the ones accuracy studies usually drop. A validation study of pre-specified cut-offs, including those patients, answers whether the fast test can replace the slow one for triage.

response.overview: Single-centre diagnostic accuracy study validating pre-specified cut-offs of two bedside tests against the exercise-test anaerobic threshold in consecutive adults booked for major abdominal surgery.
response.population: Consecutive adults booked for colorectal, upper gastrointestinal, liver or pancreatic resection who attend pre-assessment at least three weeks before surgery; excluded are patients for whom exercise testing is contraindicated.
response.exposure: Index tests at pre-assessment by a physiotherapist: 30-second sit-to-stand (cut-off 10 or fewer) and four-metre gait speed (cut-off below 1.0 m/s), both pre-specified.
response.procedures: Exercise testing within two weeks by an exercise physiologist blind to the bedside results; the physiotherapist is blind to exercise results because testing follows. Anaerobic threshold is read by two physiologists independently, with a third for disagreement. Patients who start but cannot complete exercise testing are classified as reference positive (low functional capacity) in the primary analysis. Prehabilitation allocation continues by current practice during the study.

response.title: Accuracy of bedside tests against the exercise-test anaerobic threshold for triage to prehabilitation before major abdominal surgery
response.abstract: Objective: to validate pre-specified cut-offs of the 30-second sit-to-stand test and gait speed for a low anaerobic threshold. Design: consecutive-patient accuracy study with blinded testers. Primary outcome: sensitivity of sit-to-stand 10 or fewer. Results will be written after recruitment.
response.introduction: Exercise testing is too slow to triage every patient for prehabilitation before major abdominal surgery. Bedside tests are fast, but their published cut-offs were derived in their own data and never validated.
response.methods: Consecutive adults did both bedside tests at pre-assessment and exercise testing within two weeks, with testers blind to each other's results. Patients unable to complete exercise testing were classified by a pre-specified rule, and cut-offs were fixed before recruitment.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present the flow of patients, cross-tables for each test, sensitivity and specificity with intervals, and results for patients aged 75 and over.
response.discussion: The discussion will compare validated accuracy with the published estimates and state whether bedside triage is acceptable for allocating places. It will consider the patients who could not complete either test.
response.limitations: This is a single centre, and blinding depends on the order of testing. The prevalence of the target condition may differ from the planning value.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis. It will state whether the pre-specified cut-off meets the triage threshold.
